t: like the membrane of an egg. The thin layer stuck to the inside of the eggshell (Tiferet Yisrael, Negaim 1:1).
and above. All brighter shades of white.
duller. Darker.
bohak. A white appearance that is not a leprous mark and is pure (see Leviticus 13:39).
and four appearances. Four different shades of white.
it is called baheret... se'et... sapachat. Mentioned in Leviticus 13:2.
like clean wool of a lamb born that day. Washed wool sheared from a lamb born today, whose wool has not yet had time to get very dirty (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 1:1).
like the plaster of the Sanctuary. Like the shade of the Temple walls.
is a derivative of baheret. An appendage of the baheret mark.
for the word sapachat means only an appendage. The word “sapachat” mentioned in the passage on leprous marks comes to teach that the baheret and se'et have appendages.
whether at the end of the weeks. At the end of the first or second week of quarantine (see below, halakhah 10).
and whether after the leper was released. That the priest declared him pure.
or confirmed. That the priest declared him impure.
if so, why did the Sages count them etc.. Since they all combine with one another, for what purpose did they count them under separate names.
he may not see the mark until he understands and recognizes etc.. See also below 9:2.
it is called patuch. From the root “p-t-ch”, which in Aramaic means to mix.

the patuch in the baheret is the fourth appearance etc.. For the brighter the whiteness, the more drops of blood must be in it for the redness to be noticeable in it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 1:2).
like one of the growths that come up on the body. Pimples or freckles and the like.
deeper than the skin of the flesh. As explained in Leviticus 13:3.
and not deep to the touch. It does not mean deep so that it can be felt by hand.
like the appearance of the sun, which looks to the eye deeper than the shade. For sunlight on the ground looks lower than the shade beside it.
whether leprosy of garments. Explained below in chapters 12-13 (but for leprosy of houses the measure is two grains, below 14:1).

like a Cilician grain, which is square. A gris is a bean split in two. This measure is measured in beans from the place called Cilicia, which are large and tend toward a square shape (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 6:1; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 5:7, Tosefta there 3:15). When the bean is split in two lengthwise, its inner surface is flat and smooth and convenient to measure (and it does not mean that the mark must be square in shape, but that it must have the measure from which a square of this measure can be drawn).

the amount for the growth of thirty-six hairs. An area of skin in which thirty-six hairs can grow, taking into account also the space between them (and in today's measures its size is a square whose sides are about 20 mm).
and a baheret that is dark. Whitish but darker than the egg membrane, which is not impure (as above, halakhah 1).
white hair. Its laws will be explained below in chapter 2.
and the living flesh. Its laws will be explained below in chapter 3.
and the spreading. Its laws will be explained below in chapter 4.
and all three are specified in the Torah. In the passage on leprous marks (Leviticus 13).

he shall quarantine for seven days... this is confirmed. During the days of quarantine the person is called a “quarantined leper”, and when he is declared impure he is called a “confirmed leper”, and their laws are explained below 10:6-12.
if so, what is this that is stated in the Torah. Regarding the priest's examination at the end of the second week of the mark's quarantine.

and likewise if it did not fade and did not spread etc.. That is, not only when the mark fades is he purified, but also if the mark did not spread and no other signs of impurity developed in it after two weeks of quarantine, he is purified.
so that they can be taken with tweezers. That they are long enough to be taken with scissors (Rabbi Y. Kafih explained, based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 4:4, that it refers to tweezers).
their root. The place where the hairs grow.
exact. A precise measure.
the place of the black hair does not reduce it. The place where the black hair grows does not diminish the measure of the gris.

and whether they were at the end of the baheret. At its edge, so that it does not surround them on all sides (unlike living flesh, which must be surrounded on all sides in order to be impure - below 3:1).
defiles in any appearance. Unlike the whiteness of the baheret, which defiles only from the egg membrane and above (above 1:1).
a boil or a burn. Wounds in the skin of the flesh, which as long as they are fresh do not become impure with leprous marks (see below 5:1-3).
bohak. A white appearance duller than the four defiling appearances (above 1:1).

the living flesh of the boil or the living flesh of the burn. A boil and a burn that began to heal, and then become impure with leprous marks (below 5:4; and see Mirkevet HaMishneh and Arukh HaShulchan 83:3-5, who explain why they are not defiled because of the hair in them).
and this is like a baheret that has no white hair, and he quarantines. As above 1:10.
and even though the baheret surrounds the boil etc.. Since hairs do not grow in the body of a baheret, this is not a sign of impurity.
and likewise if there was a boil... surrounding the two white hairs. Even though they themselves grow from within the baheret.
or adjacent to them at their side. That the boil or its fellow is attached to the two hairs and separates them from the baheret.
or divided between the two hairs. That the boil or its fellow divides the baheret into two so that each hair is in a different part (Tiferet Yisrael, Negaim 1:5).
and if they went away he declares him pure. As with any mark that remains unchanged at the end of the second week (above 1:11).
and it turned the hair white. This implies that the baheret must cause it.
and he was confirmed by it. The mark was confirmed impure because of the hair.
hair of deposit. From the word “pikadon” (deposit), as though the baheret deposited the hair in the place (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 5:3).
until one baheret turns two hairs. Until a single baheret the size of a gris causes the growth of two hairs, and here only half of the present baheret turned the hair.
and a baheret like half a gris was born to it with one hair in it, he quarantines. Since only the second hair was turned white by the baheret, there is no sign of impurity here.
living flesh. Ordinary skin of the flesh without baheret, which when it appears in the center of the baheret and is surrounded by it is considered a sign of impurity.
like a square lentil. The size of a lentil, which is round, except that one adds to it the corners, and in this squaring they measure (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 6:1).
the amount for the growth of four hairs. The measure of an area of skin in which four hairs can grow, taking into account also the space between them.
like a mustard seed. The size of a mustard seed, which is smaller than a lentil.
provided that the white is not from the four appearances we explained. Above 1:2, in which case it is a baheret and not living flesh.
until it is in the body of a baheret; how etc.. The whole halakhah was explained above 2:4-5 regarding white hair.
their living flesh. The living flesh of the boil and the burn.
living flesh is always a sign of impurity etc.. Unlike white hair (above 2:6).

this that is stated in the Torah, “and it turned the hair white, and living flesh of raw flesh in the se'et”. And in a later verse it says “and the priest shall declare him impure”, and one might understand that for the mark to be impure both signs are needed.
he does not need both. It is not necessary that both be in the mark to make it impure; one of them is enough.
and it is not stated white hair with the living flesh but etc.. For white hair as a sign of impurity was already mentioned alone in the earlier verses.
that it be enough to receive white hair, which is two hairs. Along its length and width (above, halakhah 1).
exactly like a gris. Exactly the size of a gris, which is the minimum measure of baheret (above 1:7).
or the living flesh diminished, he is pure. In this case the baheret is not quarantined, because a baheret from which the signs of impurity have gone is no longer quarantined (below 4:8).
increased. Grew.
the living flesh diminished from what it was. That the living flesh smaller than a lentil did not grow but diminished even more than its measure.
it is as it was. And the baheret is quarantined.
and there is no sign of impurity here. And we do not say that it is considered spreading, since the mark does not spread inward into itself (below 4:1).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
and living flesh the size of a lentil or more surrounds it from outside. A band of living flesh at least a lentil wide surrounds the baheret.
and the outer baheret to confirm, since the living flesh is in its middle. The inner baheret does not disqualify the living flesh from being a sign of impurity for the outer baheret.
on the head of a limb of the limbs. Detailed below.
and these are the heads of limbs etc.. This list appears for another matter in Hilchot Avadim 5:5.
and the tops of the ears. The entire rim of the ear.
and the head of the corona. The head of the male organ.
and the tips of the breasts of a woman. The nipples.
and a wart and flaps. Living flesh found on the head of a wart or flaps of flesh coming out of the body.
whose place sits as a gris. That have a flat area the size of a gris.
defiles in any amount. Even if the mark spread a small amount it is impure.
from one of the appearances of the marks. Those mentioned above 1:2.
less than a lentil. That does not have the measure that defiles under the law of living flesh.
he does not confirm. The priest does not make him a confirmed leper.
the baheret does not spread into the boil etc.. See also below 5:5, 6:2.

nor to the head nor to the beard even though they became bald and the hair went from them. The head and beard become impure through baheret only when all the hair has fallen from them (below 5:8-9, 5:11), and in any case they do not spread to the skin of the flesh and the skin of the flesh does not spread into them (below 5:10, 6:2).
in the skin. This implies the skin of the flesh only.

but a baheret that spread into the bohak is spreading. Although spreading itself that appears duller than the four appearances (bohak) does not defile, when the baheret spreads into the bohak and that bohak becomes one of the four appearances, this is spreading (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 6:6).
who separated between the mother and the spreading. That separated between the original mark and its spreading.
he quarantined it and they went away. And in their place a baheret came.

it is pure. Since no gris-sized part remained of the mother, there is no spreading here (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 4:8). And not even a new mark that must be seen as at the beginning, since the half gris remaining from the mother is considered as if it is not there, and in the spreading itself there is no measure of a mark (Tiferet Yisrael there).
and he quarantines week after week. As with a mark in the skin of the flesh that comes at first (above 1:10).
at the end of the days of quarantine. Within the days of quarantine.
it is as it was. For this is not considered a new mark seen at the beginning, but the same mark that was here before and stood unchanged a whole week, and therefore it is quarantined another week.
he quarantines. And does not confirm, for the spreading defiles only when the priest sees it at the end of the quarantine.
a baheret like a gris. And the priest saw it and quarantined it.
it is seen as at the beginning. Since the mother went away, this spreading has no significance, but the mark is to be seen with the signs of impurity in it as though they came at the beginning.
it is in doubt whether it is the same. And so there is defiling spreading here.
it is in doubt whether another came in its place. And there is a new mark here that must be seen as at the beginning.
and a thread coming out of it. A thin strip of baheret like a thread extends from it.
it obligates it to white hair and spreading. That if white hair grew in this thread or it spread, the baheret is impure.
for living flesh is not a sign of impurity until the baheret surrounds it etc.. As explained above 3:1.
he combines them. And they are considered one mark.
a baheret that became pure during quarantine... one never quarantines it again. But if signs of impurity developed in it he confirms, as above.
or it spread and returned to what it was. And the priest did not see in the meantime.
it remains in its purity. For one does not quarantine after a declaration of purity.
and white hair within living flesh. For in such a case it does not defile (see above 2:2).
and he confirmed it. Because of the living flesh in it.
the living flesh went away. And now the hair is inside the baheret.
the white hair went away. But the living flesh did not go away.
and the hair went away and another white hair returned. And the priest did not see in the meantime.
it is in its impurity as it was. Even without the priest seeing the new sign (see Tiferet Yisrael, Negaim 5:2).
and the skin peeled off. Flaked off.
with embers. Ashes of coals.
scab or chazazit. Kinds of skin diseases.
shachefet and kadachat. Kinds of diseases that produce pus and swelling in the skin.
if its head was blunt. Not sharp; in such a case it is reasonable that the burn came from the heat of the spit and not from the force of the blow or stab.
in the waters of Tiberias. Hot springs.
in olive refuse. The residue of olives after the oil has been pressed from them, which heats up by itself (see Hilchot Shabbat 4:1).
as long as they are fresh wounds. That not even a little skin has yet formed over them.
they are called mordin. They are called so figuratively because these places in the body recoil from being touched because of the pain (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 6:8).
as we have explained. Above 1:10.
and a crust forms on them like the peel of garlic. A thin layer of skin.

and they become impure through two signs, white hair or spreading. But they do not become impure through living flesh, since living flesh is the skin of healthy flesh (see the explanation above 3:1) and it never appears on a boil or a burn as long as they have not healed completely (Rash, Negaim 9:1).
or it spread. That the baheret spread within the boil or burn.
therefore the verse divided them. Into two different cases in two different passages (see Leviticus 13:18-28).
and a baheret the size of a gris in both of them. A baheret of the measure of a gris in both together.
for it is not fit for white hair. For hair does not grow on the palm of the hand.
nor for spreading. For the baheret in a boil does not spread into the skin of the flesh.
if it is not known whether it was a boil or a burn, it matters not at all. For example, where there is certainly only one of them and not both together.
for both are one sign and one impurity. Both become impure in the same way, and therefore there is no need to know whether it is a boil or a burn.
he shall be seen as at the beginning. As though there were a new mark here.
from the crown. The highest place on the head.
to the vertebra of the neck. The first vertebra of the neck.
to opposite his forehead. To the beginning of the forehead.
for it is said of them, “like the appearance of leprosy of the skin of the flesh”. From here they are equal to leprosy of the skin of the flesh, whose quarantine period is two weeks (above 1:10).
they do not combine with each other. So that if there is a baheret the size of a gris in both together, he is pure.
this teaches that they are two. Separate, and the whole head is not considered one place.
nor to the rest of the skin of the flesh. Outside their boundaries (see above 5:8).
or the beard that became bald. For it too becomes impure through baheret (see also below 6:2, 8:12).
they become impure like a boil and a burn in the skin of the flesh. As explained above 5:4.
except that they do not become impure through white hair. Therefore a boil and burn in them become impure only through spreading.
before hair grows on them. For example, in infants and children.
flaps. Pieces of flesh or skin hanging from the body that have no hair.
and likewise the beard of a woman etc.. The place of the beard, the chin.
and a eunuch. Who ordinarily does not grow a beard (see Hilchot Ishut 2:13).
as will be explained. Below 8:1.
and the folds. The creases of the flesh.
and under the breast. The fold beneath the protruding breast.
and the head and beard that have hair on them. Which become impure not through baheret but only through nesek (scall; below chapter 8).
and the morid boil and burn. That are still fresh wounds and do not become impure with leprous marks (above 5:3).
and they do not combine for marks. For if there is a mark in them, it does not combine with a mark in the skin of the flesh to complete it to the measure of a gris.

and they do not defile through living flesh. In a case where the mark surrounds them, they are not considered living flesh that defiles the mark through living flesh (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 6:8).

and they do not prevent one who turned entirely white. For a person whose leprosy broke out over his whole body is pure (below 7:1), even though it did not break out in these places (and see also there, halakhah 6).
those that are not skin. Such as the nail, the head and beard, and the morid boil and burn.
and the redness of the lips is judged as a hidden place. Since it is covered when the mouth is closed.
as we have explained. Above 5:4, 5:11.
and they do not combine with one another etc.. See also above 5:5.
and they do not defile through living flesh. In a case where the mark in the skin of the flesh surrounds them, they are not considered living flesh that defiles the mark through living flesh.
but they prevent one who turned entirely white. Because they are capable of becoming impure with baheret (see below 7:6).
a baheret adjacent etc.. That is attached to them in such a way that there is no other skin between them.
the mark in the skin of the flesh. This implies that the mark is surrounded on all sides by the skin of the flesh.

a gentile who had a baheret and converted, or a fetus that was born. A gentile and a fetus do not become impure with leprous marks (below 9:1), and although the baheret is still in their skin after conversion or birth, it does not defile.
in a fold and it became exposed. For example, in a fat person who became thin so that the folds of his flesh are exposed (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 7:1).
before hair ever grew on them. In which case they become impure like the skin of the flesh (above 5:11).
and its place became a boil or a burn. And now the baheret in them does not become impure (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 7:1).
whether they intensified. Became brighter.
or they faded. But did not fade below the four appearances of marks.
every doubt about marks... is pure. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 15:4.
except for the two doubts we already counted. Above 2:9, 4:6.
requires impurity. Is confirmed.

for although it is certain that the mark spread in this one etc.. Even in the case where the two bahareyot are on one person, and in any case one of his marks spread, he does not become impure thereby since it is not known which of his marks spread.
both returned to being the size of a sela, for the spreading went away from one of them. But in the second there is still spreading as long as it does not return to the size of a gris.
and it has white hair that preceded the baheret. In which case this is not a sign of impurity (above 2:6).
and he does not know which was first from which turned. He does not know how to distinguish between the pure hair and the hair that is a sign of impurity.
if during quarantine he became uncertain. And likewise if he became uncertain in a case that came at the beginning.
and before he confirms him and says to him “you are impure”. For as long as the priest does not say “impure” he is not impure (below 9:2).
if it was at the beginning or at the end of the first week, he quarantines etc.. As with a baheret that has no signs of impurity (above 1:10).
whether at the beginning or after quarantine. Whether he was confirmed at the start or confirmed after quarantine.
or he was quarantined. And not confirmed at all, since no signs of impurity developed in it.
like the law of a small baheret. See above 1:10.
and both of them shrank or one of them. So that they do not have the measure that defiles (see above 2:1).
the boil was adjacent to both etc.. In all these cases the hair is not considered a sign of impurity (ibid. halakhah 4).

another white hair was born... he is impure because it came entirely white at the beginning. For had it broken out entirely after quarantine he would be pure even if another white hair was born to him afterward (below, halakhah 3 - Tiferet Yisrael, Negaim 8:7).
in the four appearances of white and the four of patuch. These are the appearances of the defiling marks (see above 1:2, 1:4).
as we have explained. There, halakhah 5.

or the living flesh went away first and afterward it broke out over all of him. For example, where the priest did not see him in the meantime, so that the breaking out did not occur after a declaration of purity (Kesef Mishneh).

and even if white hair was born to him. Although white hair defiles one who comes at the beginning entirely white (above, halakhah 2), it does not defile a mark that breaks out from quarantine or confirmation.
as it is stated. Regarding leprosy that broke out.
and it must be the size of a square lentil or more. Which is the measure that defiles through living flesh (above 3:1).
even the tops of limbs, which do not defile through living flesh. As explained above 3:8.
to bohak. A white appearance darker than the egg membrane that does not become impure with marks (above 1:1).

if flesh returned in the appearance of bohak, he is pure. Although bohak is not considered leprosy and therefore prevents one who turned entirely white, it is also not considered living flesh, and therefore its return does not make this person impure and he remains pure.
and anything not fit to become impure with a baheret mark. That is among the places that do not become impure with baheret (listed above 6:1).

or less than a lentil of living flesh remained adjacent to the boil... he is pure. For just as these places do not prevent the breaking out, so they do not combine with living flesh to complete it to the measure of a lentil.
for they are fit for baheret. And therefore they prevent one who turned entirely white (although they do not combine with the skin of the flesh and do not defile through living flesh, as above 6:2).
and one pure. For example, one after a declaration of purity.

he is pure, because he was confirmed impure, even though it was the pure one that broke out. Although one who breaks out after a declaration of purity is impure (above, halakhah 2), since the person was confirmed impure because of the impure baheret, it is considered breaking out from confirmation, and he is pure.

and not only that, but even if one was on his upper lip and one on his lower lip etc.. For example, he has one impure baheret above the mouth or above the eye and one pure baheret beneath them, and when the mouth or eye is closed they look like one large baheret.
the two bahareyot look like one baheret. And one could treat the case as though there is only one pure baheret here (see the rulings and opinions).

since it broke out over all of him, he is pure. For here too the person was impure because of the impure baheret, and therefore it is considered breaking out from confirmation and he is pure (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 8:6, who explained this law differently).

he did not manage to show him to the priest until it broke out over all of him, he is pure. Since he did not show the priest the baheret after the signs of impurity went from it, he is still in his impurity (see below 9:3), and therefore it is considered a mark that broke out from confirmation, which is pure (above, halakhah 1).

whereas had he first shown the priest and he declared him pure... he would have been confirmed, as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1, that one who breaks out after a declaration of purity is impure.

and he did not manage to show him to the priest until it broke out over all of him, he is impure and requires quarantine. Since he showed the priest only after it broke out over all of him, he is like one who came at the beginning entirely white, whose law is quarantine (above, halakhah 2).
whereas had he first shown the priest and he quarantined him... he would have been pure, as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1, that one who breaks out from quarantine is pure.
and a nesek is no less than a square gris. Which is the measure of all leprous marks (above 1:7).
whether its appearance was deep. As explained above regarding leprosy of the skin of the flesh (ibid. halakhah 6).
and the woman and the eunuch. Whose beard does not ordinarily grow hair.
and all this is specified in the Torah. Leviticus 13:29-37.
he shall shave around the nesek but not shave the nesek. As explained below, halakhah 3.
and he leaves two hairs adjacent to it. He leaves two hairs around the nesek on every side, so that the nesek is surrounded by a ring of hair.

so that the spreading will be recognizable. For if these hairs fall out, it is a sign that the nesek spread (the measure of spreading being two hairs, Raavad on Sifra, Tazria, beginning of parashah 5).
and his shaving is valid by anyone... and likewise with anything. Unlike the shaving of purification, which is valid only by a priest and with a razor (below 11:3).
and even if he was a nazirite, he shaves. Although a nazirite is forbidden to cut his hair (Hilchot Nezirut 1:1), he is permitted this shaving (see Mishneh LaMelekh).
like the form of gold. Like the color of gold.
it need only be short. And even so it must have the minimum measure of hair (below, halakhah 5, and see the rulings and opinions).
whether they were at the end of the nesek. At its edge.
whether the yellow hair preceded the nesek. Unlike white hair in a baheret, which defiles only when the baheret preceded it (above 2:6).
as we have explained regarding white hair. Above 2:1.
the black hair that saves in scalls. That prevents them from becoming impure (as explained in the next paragraph).
enough to bend their heads to their roots. A length sufficient to bend the tips of the hairs to their roots (a longer measure than hairs that can be taken with tweezers).
for what grows saves anywhere. Even at the edge of the nesek.
from the standing hair. The hair outside the nesek.
and one short. That does not bend its head to its root.
he is confirmed as he was. And he need not be shown to the priest as at the beginning (and compare above 4:11).
and a row. A line.
it is as it was. For the nesek is not purified by the black hair between them.
for the black hair that remains between them is at the side of the nesek. And remaining black hair saves only when it is in the middle of the nesek (above, halakhah 6).
if the row was breached in two places he is pure etc.. For now the two nesek patches look like one nesek with black hair inside it.
no less than the place where two hairs grow. For at this measure the hair is considered to be in the middle of the nesek (ibid.).

and if the breach in one place was the size of a gris, he is impure etc.. For since one of the two breaches has the measure of a gris, it is considered a nesek in itself with no black hair in it (and see the illustration for a possible understanding of the case).
and another nesek surrounds the black hair. And this outer nesek is pure since there is black hair in its middle.
for the inner nesek and the outer have become one nesek. And therefore the breach of a gris is not considered a nesek in itself (unlike the previous case; see Rikevo).
provided that the breach is the amount for the growth of two hairs or more. For only from this measure onward do the two nesek patches look like one nesek.
that had a thread coming out of it. A thin strip of nesek extends from it like a thread.
obligates them to become impure through thin yellow hair and spreading. That if thin yellow hair grew in this thread or it spread, the nesek is impure (similar to above 4:7 regarding baheret).
and saves them by what grows in it. That if black hair grew in it, it saves the nesek patches.

but remaining black hair... does not save unless the width of the thread is a gris. A place of six by six hairs (above 1:7). For the remaining hair saves only if it is at a distance of two hairs on every side from the attached hair (above, halakhah 6).
but less than two hairs. For one hair does not prevent the whole scall from being impure (see Mikdash David, Taharot 50).
he is pure. Similar to the law of a baheret that broke out over all of him (above chapter 7, Tosefta Negaim 4:6).
or after a declaration of purity. Unlike a baheret that broke out over all of him after a declaration of purity, which is confirmed impure (above 7:1), regarding scalls even in this case he is pure.
it is a tradition. A tradition of the Sages.
and the skin of the beard that became bald becomes impure with marks of the skin of the flesh. Just as the head that became bald becomes impure with them.
as we have explained. Above 5:11, 6:2.
one who came at the beginning... quarantines one week. Similar to the law of one who came at the beginning entirely white with no signs of impurity, who requires quarantine (above 7:2).
pure, as we have explained. In the previous paragraph.

the black hair went away, he is impure because of spreading. Although a nesek in which black hair was born is considered healed and remains pure even after the hair goes away (above, halakhah 8), this applies only to one purified from confirmation, but not to one purified from quarantine (Raavad and Rikevo). Perhaps this law is stated specifically in the case of one who came entirely scalled, where unlike other scalls there are no other hairs apart from this one that grew, and therefore its going away is considered spreading.
they do not prevent each other. So that if the whole head became scalled (after it was seen by the priest) he is pure, even though the beard did not become scalled, and vice versa.
and they do not combine with each other. So that if there is a nesek the size of a gris only when both combine, he is pure.
from the joint of the upper jaw. The bone of the upper cheek.
the bulge of the throat. The protrusion in the throat (the upper ring of the windpipe).
he stretches a thread from ear to ear etc.. In order to estimate the boundary of the beard at the front of the face.
a resident alien. A gentile who lives in the Land of Israel and accepted upon himself to keep the seven Noahide commandments (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6).
and all are fit to see the marks. And not only priests (as below, halakhah 2).
and all marks a person may see. Even those of his wife and relatives.
a priest who does not know how to see. Who is not expert in examining marks.
until his teacher instructs him and he is expert in all the marks and their names. See also above 1:3.
he is impure, and the priest declared him impure etc.. This implies that only if he is truly impure is the priest permitted to declare him impure, and likewise regarding purification.
in the place of the mark. In the place where the impure mark was.
and the second cannot declare him impure through spreading, because he does not know etc.. Since only the first priest saw the mark at the beginning in its original size.

and a priest is believed to say etc.. For example, where the first priest, before he died or fell ill, said that the mark had spread and the like, in which case the second priest may rely on his words (Arukh HaShulchan 93:10).
a chalal. One born to a priest and a woman forbidden to him, or whose father was a chalal (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:1-10, 19:14).
in their priesthood. And a chalal is not considered a priest but a non-priest (ibid. halakhah 10).
but those with blemishes are fit to see marks. Although they are unfit for service in the Temple (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 6:1-7).
blind. Sightless.
whose eyesight dimmed. His vision weakened.
to all the appearance of the priest's eyes. This implies that the priest's vision must be complete.
in the whole matter. In the passage on marks.
and not inside the house. When speaking of marks of people or garments, or even marks of houses when the windows of the house are closed and it is dark (Tosafot Yom Tov, Negaim 2:2).
because a dim one looks bright. These times or places are somewhat dark, and therefore a dim baheret appears brighter in them than it is.
nor at noon. When the day is brightest.
in the fourth and fifth hour and in the eighth and ninth. At these hours the day is neither too bright nor too dark (referring to seasonal hours).

except on the Sabbath and festivals. Because examining marks is considered a judgment, and one does not judge on the Sabbath and festivals (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 1:4; see Hilchot Shabbat 23:14).
the seventh day fell. Of the quarantine, on which the mark is examined (above 1:10 and elsewhere).

as it is stated, “and the priest shall command, and they shall empty the house”. Regarding leprosy of a house it says that the priest commands to empty it before he rules it impure, so that the vessels in it will not become impure as the vessels of a leprous house do (see below 16:1-6) and great loss be caused to the owner of the house.

if the Torah waited for a matter of choice so that his vessels not become impure. That the loss and trouble of the homeowner whose vessels became impure is a matter of choice, and nevertheless the Torah took it into account.
all the more so for a matter of a mitzvah. Such as a groom's joy or the joy of a festival.
we give him all seven days of the feast. We do not examine his mark during this time, lest he be found impure and the joy of the wedding be impaired.
we give him all the days of the festival. “Lest he be found impure and his festival turn into mourning” (Hilchot Yom Tov 7:16).
or on the thirteenth day. After two weeks of quarantine.

because the seventh day counts toward the first week and toward the second week. For the seventh day is considered both the last day of the first quarantine and the first day of the second quarantine.
we do not quarantine within the days of quarantine. If another mark was born to him within the days of quarantine.
and we do not confirm one already confirmed if another mark was born to him etc.. Rather we wait until he is purified from the first mark, and then examine the second mark.

and he saw this one and again saw this one... whether at the beginning, at the end of the first week, or at the end of the second week. For at the times of examining marks one may examine two marks one after the other.
and one does not see two marks at once. To examine both simultaneously.
and the priest shall see the mark. And not “the marks”.
to search. To look for the mark.
under the armpits of the afflicted. In the armpit.
his thighs. His testicles.
or in the folds. Between the creases of the flesh.
to all the appearance of the priest's eyes. This implies only what can be seen openly without effort (and compare above 6:1).
and likewise with one who turned entirely white. That these places do not prevent one who turned entirely white.
and how does he stand before the priest. In what manner does the afflicted stand so that the marks visible in this position are considered exposed.

and he stands like one who hoes and like one who gathers olives. The man stands as if hoeing the ground and as if picking olives, in order to see the marks on various parts of his body (see the rulings and opinions).
and she sits like one who kneads. As if kneading dough.
and like one who weaves on upright looms. On weaving implements that stand on the ground.
she raises her right hand until the armpit is exposed. For one who weaves on upright looms ordinarily raises her right hand a little in this way.
so he is seen for his shaving. For in the purification process the leper must shave all the hair of his body.
as will be explained. Below 11:1.
one who plucks signs of impurity. For example, white hair from the baheret.
or one who burns the living flesh. For living flesh that is burned is no longer considered living flesh and does not defile (Rosh, Negaim 7:4, and see Hilchot Shechitah 7:15).
for he is impure as he was. For there is still a sign of impurity in the mark.
flogging for rebelliousness. Lashes by rabbinic law.

and likewise one who shaves the nesek. Who shaves the yellow hair from the nesek and thereby nullifies the signs of impurity (Mirkevet HaMishneh, and see Maimonides, Sefer HaMitzvot, negative commandment 307). Some explain that it means he shaves the hairs adjacent to the nesek, in which case the spreading is not recognizable (Raavad, and see above 8:3).
and to tie the sivin on his foot. The cord used to tie the shoe on his afflicted foot (Rashi, Shabbat 133a).
he is pure. And is not confirmed impure because of the signs of impurity he plucked (though it appears that if a baheret remained, the priest quarantines him).
he is pure after the days of quarantine. For after the days of quarantine have passed on him, if no new signs of impurity were born to him he is pure.
he is confirmed as he was. For he is not purified by the going away of the signs of impurity, since he plucked them himself.
and he has no purity until it breaks out etc.. For in these ways the mark can become pure without taking the signs of impurity into account.

if he cut off all the living flesh that surrounds it... he has no purity ever. Since he cut off the baheret, it is impossible to know whether it went away from him or shrank below a gris, and likewise it is impossible to know whether the leprosy broke out over all of him, since perhaps it did not spread in the hair that was plucked and which prevents it (Kesef Mishneh).

one who plucks a single white hair... he is pure. Although a confirmed person who plucks signs of impurity remains in his impurity (above, halakhah 2), in this case he is pure since he is purified anyway because of the falling out of the second hair.

he plucked two and one fell out, he is in his impurity. For had he not plucked, he would have remained impure, and therefore his law is that of a confirmed person who plucks signs of impurity, who remains impure. And likewise regarding one who burns the living flesh.
he circumcises. Even though he cuts off the baheret thereby.

for a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment. Therefore the positive commandment of circumcision overrides the negative commandment of cutting off the baheret (and see also Hilchot Milah 1:9).
and if he circumcised and the sign by which he was confirmed went away with the foreskin. If by cutting off the baheret in the place of the foreskin the signs of impurity went away.
he is liable for the leper's offering. Like a confirmed leper who was healed of his leprosy (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:1).
like a mourner. Just as a mourner is obligated to cover his head and wrap his mustache (Hilchot Evel 5:19).
and tears his garments. Rends them.

as it is stated, “and the leper in whom is the mark”, etc.. And the rest of the verse: “his garments shall be torn, and his head shall be unkempt, and he shall cover his mustache, and he shall cry, ‘Impure! Impure!’”
even a High Priest. Who is forbidden to let his hair grow wild and to tear his garments even when he is a mourner (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:6).
lets his hair grow wild. Like the law of the leper, who is forbidden to cut his hair (as explained explicitly in the next paragraph).

for a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment. Therefore the commandment of letting the leper's hair grow and tearing his garments overrides the prohibition of the High Priest's letting his hair grow and tearing garments.
and he is forbidden to greet... like a mourner. Hilchot Evel 5:20.
reads, learns, and expounds. Unlike a mourner (ibid. halakhah 16).
and he is forbidden to cut hair and launder. Just as a mourner is forbidden to do so (ibid. halakhah 1).
even on Sabbaths and festivals. For mourning does not apply on them regarding public matters (ibid. 10:1, 10:3).
but he is permitted to wash, anoint, etc.. Although a mourner is forbidden these things (ibid. 5:1).
and marital relations. Only during the days of his confirmation, but during the seven days he counts after his shaving he is forbidden marital relations (see below 11:1).
and he sets up his bed like the rest of the people. Unlike a mourner, who must overturn his bed (Hilchot Evel 5:18).
and this matter applies only in walled cities in the Land of Israel. For these cities are holier than the rest of the land (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:13).
and a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered over, so it is not evident whether he is male or female. [Note: Maimonides in the Commentary on the Mishnah vocalizes this word: tumtom.]
and an androginos. One who has both male and female sexual organs.
because it is a doubt. See also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:4.
but only letting hair grow wild and tearing garments. And the same applies to wrapping the mustache (Tosafot Yom Tov, Megillah 1:7), for a quarantined leper is exempt from all of these.
and shaving and birds. For the leper is obligated to shave all his hair and bring two birds as part of his purification process (see below 11:1).
but the impurity of both is equal in every respect. As explained in the following halakhot.
defiles a person and vessels by touch. Like any primary source of impurity (Hilchot Tumat Met 5:7).
and earthenware vessels by air space. For an earthenware vessel becomes impure when impurity enters its hollow (ibid. 1:5, Hilchot Kelim 13:1).
and defiles a person by carrying. A person who carries the leper becomes impure even if the leper does not touch him (Hilchot Tumat Met 1:9).

and defiles a couch and seat even under the stone, like a zav and zavah. Even when the leper sits on a stone, he defiles the couch and seat beneath it (as below 13:13), just as zavim and zavot defile in this way (see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 6:5, and see the rulings and opinions).
they learned from tradition. The tradition of the Sages in interpreting the verses.
and they become a first-degree impure. Like one who touches a primary source of impurity (Hilchot Tumat Met 5:8).
even his seat is impure. And everything found with him in the same house is considered his seat.
and the leper passed under it, it did not defile it. Since the leper did not stand but only passed, the tree is not considered his “seat”.
in doubt whether he stood or did not stand, it is pure. This is one of the twelve doubts that the Sages ruled pure (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 14:1, 15:5).
and most of him. Most of his body.
four cubits by four cubits wide. By means of the partition a separate area of four cubits by four cubits is made for him.

so that his seat is alone and he does not stand mixed with the people and defile them. Through the partition the leper is not in the same seat as the rest of the people, and therefore does not defile them; and so as not to defile the people by his walking from the entrance to the partition, he enters first and leaves last (Rash, Negaim 13:12).
an earthenware bowl. An earthenware vessel.
and it is a tradition. A tradition of the Sages.

living water fit for sanctifying the sin-offering waters. Spring water (unlike rainwater) fit for sanctifying the ashes of the red heifer (see Hilchot Parah 6:1, and for their definition see there, halakhot 10-16).
the better of the two. The more select (in case they are not entirely equal; see below, halakhah 8).
and squeezes. Squeezes the blood out of the bird.
and its thickness is a quarter of a leg of the legs of a bed. A quarter of the thickness of one of the legs of a bed.
as we have explained. In Hilchot Parah 11:5.
it is no less than a handbreadth. Its length.
and scarlet wool whose weight is a shekel. Wool dyed with the scarlet worm (for its dyeing see Hilchot Parah 3:2) weighing one shekel.

and if its taste disqualified it, like the dyeing of tekhelet. If he took even a little of the dye in order to test it on the wool, it is entirely disqualified for the mitzvah, as in the dyeing of tekhelet for tzitzit (see Hilchot Tzitzit 2:3).
a halakhah. Given to Moses at Sinai.
they prevent one another. For the sprinkling on the leper (as explained in the next paragraph) cannot be performed if any one of them is missing.
with a strip of scarlet. A strip of wool dyed with the scarlet worm.
and he brings the tips of the wings near them. Brings the tips of the wings close to them.
behind his hand. The back of his hand.
and throws it outside the wall. Toward the outside of the wall.
to outside the city. From here it is learned that the one sending stands inside the city (Mishneh LaMelekh).
to the face of the field. From here it is learned that he does not turn his face toward other places but toward the field.
until he becomes like a gourd. That is, smooth over his entire body.
launders his garments. Immerses them in a mikveh.
and he is purified from defiling by entry and from defiling as a couch and seat. See above 10:11-12.
and he may enter inside the wall. For until now he stayed outside the city wall (ibid. halakhah 7).
and he is like all tevulei yom. For he is second-degree impure (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:2).
and he eats maaser. He may eat second tithe (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:4).
when his sun has set he eats terumah. When evening comes he is purified regarding eating terumah (Hilchot Terumot 7:2).
when he has brought his atonement he eats sacred things. After he has brought his offerings he is permitted to eat sacred things.
as we have explained. Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1.
and it is the first. And he must count seven days anew.

the leper's shaving, his immersion, and his sprinkling do not prevent one another, but all his other acts prevent. According to most commentators there is a scribal error here and the text should be reversed: “the leper's shaving, his immersion, and his sprinkling prevent one another, and all his other acts do not prevent,” as stated in the Tosefta (Negaim 8:5; and see Kesef Mishneh, who upholds the text before us).
and all his other acts. Such as sending the birds and laundering the garments.
and all his other acts. Such as taking the birds and sending them, the immersion, and laundering the garments (see Sifra, Metzora, parashah 1, halakhah 3).
in the presence of the Temple. When the Temple exists.

as it is stated, “to purify him or to declare him impure”. From here it is a mitzvah for the priest who declares impure to be the one who purifies. From here it is also learned that this applies at all times and in all places (see Sifra, Tazria, parashah 5, chapter 16, halakhah 13).

even a zav and even one impure through a corpse. Although they are not permitted to enter the Temple, since they are permitted to enter walled cities they can purify the leper (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:1-4; and see Sifra, Metzora, parashah 1, halakhah 5).
for mitzvot are not done in bundles. See also Hilchot Rotzeach 10:5, Hilchot Avadim 3:9.
forbidden for benefit. And all the more so for eating.
for a slaughter that is not fit. For its mitzvah.
as it is stated. Regarding birds forbidden for eating.
from tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

and a negative commandment derived from a general positive commandment is a positive commandment. A prohibition not stated in the Torah in negative language, but learned from the meaning of positive wording, is not considered a negative commandment but a positive commandment.
a condemned city. A city most of whose inhabitants worship idolatry, all of whose property must be burned (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:6).
that he exchanged for idolatry. That he exchanged for idolatry, for exchanges for idolatry are forbidden for benefit like it (see ibid. 8:1, 7:9).
and not from birds that killed a person. Which are forbidden for the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:6).
in appearance, in height, and in price. In general appearance, size, and monetary value.
and their purchase as one. He should buy both together.
to purify with them a leprous house. For a leprous house also requires birds, as for the purification of a person (below 15:8).
and he shall take for the one being purified. This implies any person being purified, whoever he is.
and it turned out not to be a dror. That this bird is not of the kind called “dror”, or that this bird is not free (see the rulings and opinions above, halakhah 1).
and the first is permitted for eating. Since the bird was not fit at all for this mitzvah, it is not forbidden.
and it turned out to be a treifah. And a treifah is not fit for this mitzvah (for the definition of treifah see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:6-9).
and the first is permitted for benefit. But not for eating, since it is a treifah.
the blood was spilled. Of the bird that was slaughtered.
like leprosy of a person. Above 1:7.
and all three are specified in the Torah. See Leviticus 13:47-59.
and like the branches of a palm. The fronds of the palm.
like a fine scarlet. Wool well dyed with the scarlet worm (for its dyeing see Hilchot Parah 3:2).
which is the thirteenth day. In counting the days of quarantine, for the seventh day counts toward both weeks (see above 9:9).
if it faded to the third appearance. Which is a pure appearance, neither greenish nor reddish.
for the spreading of the mark into itself is not spreading, whether in a person etc.. As above 4:1.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
and likewise a garment in which the mark spread. Next to it, even a very small amount.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
that which has the mark in it. This implies also the garment around the mark.

they pass over them the seven agents that are passed over a stain. They pass over the mark seven different cleaning agents that are customarily passed over a stain, so that it will be laundered well and no trace of it remains (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 8:10).

in the way they pass over stains, as we have explained regarding niddah. In the same order and manner in which these agents are passed over the red stains a woman sees on her garments, to determine whether it is blood that makes her impure or a dye (Hilchot Issurei Biah 9:36-38).
and he sews a patch as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.

one who tears off from a quarantined garment onto a pure one. Tore a patch from a garment that was quarantined and became pure and sewed it onto a pure garment (Rabbi Ch. Albeck, Negaim 11:6, and see Rash there).
and the mark returned to the garment. The quarantined one, from which the patch was taken.

he examines the garment to which it is sewn by signs. The mark on the sewn patch is considered as though it appeared on the second garment itself, and he quarantines it according to the signs of impurity in it.

if it remained unchanged for two weeks or spread, they burn everything. And if it faded to the third appearance the garment is pure. But the patch itself is burned in any case, since the mark returned in it (Tosefta Negaim 5:8).
that came at the beginning entirely greenish or reddish. That the whole garment is greenish or reddish.

but a garment he quarantined, and the mark spread over all of it... or that he declared pure... is pure. Just as in marks of people, one who breaks out from impure is pure (above 7:1), except that here even one who breaks out after a declaration of purity is pure (and similarly above 8:12 regarding scalls).

it contracted and spread. If the mark that broke out over the entire garment contracted a little at the end of the first week and spread again at the end of the second week (Rash, Negaim 11:7, Rikevo).
it shall be burned. Although it broke out over all of it, and unlike a mark that breaks out in a person (see above 7:5).
that tufts came out on its surface from the weave. That small clumps of hair come out of the weave, as is common in new wool blankets (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 11:11).
sagos. A coarse cloak.

its baldness is the worn ones, its bareness the new ones. “Its baldness” is a term for old garments that are already worn and bald of their hairs, and “its bareness” is a term for new ones that have hairs (ibid.).
its warp. The warp threads that run along the length of the garment.
and its woof. The weft threads that run across its width.
wool. Sheep's wool (of ewes or rams).
and linen. Flax.
or the warp or the woof of wool and linen. Threads made of them, even though they are not woven as a garment.
skin dyed by Heaven becomes impure with marks. Unlike garments, which even if dyed by Heaven do not become impure (above 12:10).
and felts. Which are made of pieces of wool joined together that were not spun and woven.

one who buys garments from gentiles, they are seen at the beginning. Although gentiles' garments do not become impure with marks, one who buys from them a garment that has a mark must show it to the priest, and it does not remain pure (unlike marks on the body - above 6:4, and see Rash, Negaim 11:1).
a mixture of wool and linen becomes impure with marks. For it is considered a garment in every respect, except that it is forbidden to wear (see Hilchot Kilayim 10:12).
that he mixed them together. Mixed them and made a garment from them.
if most is from camels etc.. See also Hilchot Kilayim 10:6-8.
and hemp. A fiber plant similar to flax (“cultivated cannabis”).
and a ewe that was born of a goat. A goat that gave birth to an offspring that looks like a ewe.
its wool does not become impure with marks. For its wool is not considered wool regarding leprosy (and in other contexts see Hilchot Tzitzit 2:1, Hilchot Kilayim 10:2).
goat hair. Goat wool.
does not become impure with marks. Since the warp or the woof is entirely of one kind, it is recognized in the garment on its own, and therefore it does not become impure with marks (Kiryat Sefer).
skin that is not processed. That has not undergone the processing which includes salting and soaking in flour and gallnuts (see Hilchot Shabbat 18:14).
when it is raw. Raw material, even if processed.
their flat ones. Those with no receptacle.
their receptacles. Such as the wineskin and the satchel.

any amount. For a receptacle has no minimum measure regarding receiving impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 2:1), and some explain that even flat leather vessels receive marks-impurity in any amount, unlike other impurities where they must be at least five by five handbreadths (Chazon Ish, Negaim 1:25, and see Hilchot Kelim 23:3 and below, halakhah 6).
he attached to them something that grows from the ground etc.. See also Hilchot Kelim 1:3.
a cord. A thin thread.

provided that he attached it to it in the way that garments are joined for impurity. For one who sews two garments together, if one becomes impure the other is impure too (Hilchot Parah 12:5), and this is only when he attached them with more than one stitch (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 11:1, and see Hilchot Kilayim 10:24).

although it does not become impure through the midras of the zav etc.. For any vessel not used for lying or sitting does not become impure through the treading of a zav and the like (midras impurity and its laws are explained in Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav chapters 6-7).
a ship's sail. The sail of the ship.
and a net's decoration. A woolen thread hung on the hairnet (head covering) as decoration.
and barbers' cloths. Placed on the shoulders of the person being shaved during a haircut (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 11:11, Kilayim 9:3).
and straps of a shoe and sandal. For example, those that have the form of a vessel on them, for otherwise they are pure (see Hilchot Kelim 27:11 and Mishneh LaMelekh there).
that have a width of a gris. So that a mark of the measure can be seen in them.
and needless to say other vessels. That become impure through the midras of a zav.
the wineskin and the satchel. Leather bags.
are seen in their usual way. And there is no need to unfold the folds and untie the knots and the like to see the mark in them.
and the mark spreads from inside them to behind them and from behind them to inside them. For if the mark spreads from the inside outward or the reverse, it is spreading.
a creased sheet, its creases are unfolded. For that is how it ordinarily appears.
the warp and the woof. The warp threads are the thin threads forming the base of the weave, and the woof threads are the thicker threads that pass between them.
become impure with marks immediately when they are spun. Unlike other impurities, in which threads do not become impure until woven as a garment (see Hilchot Kelim 1:11-12).
even though he did not bleach the flax or boil the wool. For it was customary to bleach and boil the wool and flax even after they were spun (see Tosafot, Shabbat 27b).
in a skein of spun thread. A bundle of threads.
enough to weave from it three by three. A length of thread from which a fabric of three by three fingerbreadths can be woven (the measure of fabric that becomes impure with marks, above 12:10).
whether it was all warp or all woof. Although woof threads are thicker than warp threads, so that their skein is larger, their measure is equal.
gathered from broken threads. That are not connected to one another.
joined. Connected.
part of which is wound on the upper beam etc.. For the warp threads stretched between the upper and lower beams are wound around each of them a number of times.
and likewise two pieces of a shirt. Two pieces of cloth that when cut remained connected by a thread (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 11:9).
and the mark appeared in one of them. In one of the skeins, or one of the windings of the warp, or one of the pieces of the shirt.
the second is pure even though one thread is connected between them. For these things are not considered connected for the matter of marks.

the mark appeared in the nefesh hamasechet and in the standing warp. The woof threads inserted into the warp but not yet tightened into the fabric, but a little distant from it, are called the “nefesh of the weaving” (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 21:1), and this speaks of where the mark appears in them and in the warp threads stretched between the beams.

even though part of the mark is in the garment... he is impure. For the garment whose weaving is not yet complete (which is the nefesh hamasechet) is considered one with the warp threads (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim there, and see Chazon Ish, Negaim 1:23).
the woven fabric is pure. For unlike the nefesh hamasechet, the woven fabric is no longer considered part of the standing warp.
the threads. The threads coming out of the sheet.
the ornamental borders. Decorations on the edge of the garment.
pure. For dyed garments and gentiles' garments do not become impure with marks (above 12:10, 13:2), and even a garment that was quarantined loses its impurity.
he cut it and made it into tufts. Cut it into small pieces.
and it is permitted for benefit. Since it is pure, whereas if it were impure, even if only quarantined, it would be forbidden for benefit (Sifra, Tazria, parashah 5, chapter 14, halakhah 11).

all of them are impure and shall be burned, even one among several thousand. For a confirmed garment is already subject to impurity, and therefore its doubt is impure, unlike a quarantined garment, which is not yet subject to impurity and therefore its doubt is pure (Rash, Negaim 11:12, and see above 6:5).
like a leprous person in every respect etc.. See above 10:11-12.
even the size of an olive. The measure that defiles (below, halakhah 14).
as it is stated, “let her not be as one dead”. This was said of Miriam, who was leprous.
just as a corpse in the size of an olive. See Hilchot Tumat Met 2:1-2.
and this is a stringency in garments over a person. For a person is sent out only from walled cities (above 10:7).
like two grains side by side. Unlike the other marks, whose measure is one gris.
it turns out that the width of the mark etc.. For the measure of each gris is six hairs by six hairs (above 1:7).
in a square. That the mark looks like a rectangle whose width is six hairs and length twelve.
and all are specified in the Torah. See Leviticus 14:33-48.
the one that returns after the plastering. The mark that returns to the house after the priest removed the leprous stones and plastered the entire house (below 15:2).
the appearance of the mark is lower than the wall. That the mark appears to the eye to be sunken into the wall (see above 1:6).
and in the two appearances they quarantine or confirm. The process of quarantining the house and confirming it impure is only in these two appearances and not in other appearances.
and for spreading they demolish etc.. The house is demolished only when the mark returns after the leprous stones were removed and other stones were put in their place and the house was plastered.
as will be explained. Below 15:2.

even bundles of wood and bundles of reeds. That do not receive impurity (Rabbeinu Ovadiah of Bartenura, Negaim 12:5; the reason is that here there is a special mitzvah to empty the house; and see Mishneh LaMelekh, who wrote that regarding leprosy of a house there is a special law that even these receive impurity).
and a dark house. That has no windows.
one does not open windows in it. One does not dig in the wall to make windows in it.
until it is four cubits by four cubits. Which is the measure of a house everywhere in halakhah (see Hilchot Mezuzah 6:2, Hilchot Rotzeach 11:1, and elsewhere).
or it was built on a ship or hung on four beams. That are not attached to the ground, in which case it is not built on the land.
it was built on four pillars. That are attached to the ground.
enough to put under the lintel. A small piece of wood that is customarily placed under the lintel when it is installed (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 12:4).

enough to put between one brick and another. A “patzim” is half a brick placed in a building (ibid.; and see Otzar HaGeonim, Shabbat 82a, who explained in other ways), and earth is placed between two patzim to fill the space between them. And although these measures are very small, they are enough to make the house impure with marks.
a house one of whose sides is covered etc.. That one of the house's walls is covered with marble or rock or bricks or earth (Rikevo).
he nullified them. From the status of food that receives only light impurity, and their law is like the wood of the house (see Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 2:20).
they became impure with it with severe impurity. For they are considered a primary source of impurity like it, defiling people and vessels.
as will be explained. Below 16:1.
Jerusalem... does not become impure with marks. See also Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:14.
and Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes. And it is not the “holding” of any particular person.
whether dyed by man or dyed by Heaven. Unlike garments, which do not become impure when dyed, and skins, which do not become impure when dyed by man (above 12:10, 13:1).
the walls of the manger. Made for animals.
the partition in the house. That divides between different rooms (see Rash MiShantz, Negaim 12:4).
for the seventh day counts here and there etc.. As explained above 9:9.
words of tradition. A tradition of the Sages.
as we have explained. Above 14:2-3.
found it entirely greenish or reddish at the beginning. That the whole house is greenish or reddish.
and he purifies the house with the birds. As below, halakhah 8. But one that faded at the end of the first week does not need birds for its purification.
and he removes the earth to outside the city. The plaster that he removed from the place of the mark, he separates and takes out to outside the city.

if the mark returned the size of two grains, this is spreading after plastering. The mere return of the mark to the house after plastering is considered spreading, even though the mark returned at its original size and did not grow larger.
he removes no fewer than two stones. For the mark defiles only when it is seen on at least two stones (above 14:7).
and he does not take stones from this side. Of the house.
nor two stones in place of one removed stone. One should not bring two new stones before removing the two leprous stones (Tiferet Yisrael, Negaim 12, Boaz note 7; Mishnah Achronah, Negaim 12:6).
and he may bring two in place of three. For the main thing is not to have fewer than two stones in bringing and in removing.

if the wall was between him and his fellow, both of them remove etc.. That the neighbor who lives on the other side of the leprous wall must also help in removing the stones, scraping the earth, and bringing the new stones.
he shall take and plaster. In the singular, from which it is learned that only the owner of the house does this.
a stone in the corner. A large stone in the corner of the wall between him and his fellow that is seen on both sides.

and there is a doubt whether his fellow's part will be like a “hand” to his stone. A “yad” (handle) is something attached to food (such as the stem of a fruit used for holding it), and one who touches it is like one who touches the food itself regarding receiving impurity (see Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 5:1-2). The doubt here is whether the part of the stone in the neighbor's house will become a kind of “handle” to the other, leprous part, and so bring impurity also to the neighbor's house.
he leaves the beams for the upper room. For one does not demolish the ceiling of the house but leaves it (by supporting it with pillars and the like) for use of the upper room.
the frames. Wooden frames on the roof used as a parapet (Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 13:3, Zavim 4:2), and some explain that it means frames of windows and doors (Rash there).
window grilles. Bars.
one who takes stones from a quarantined house. This speaks not of the leprous stones but of other stones.
the mark returned to the quarantined one, he removes the stones in the pure one. For now they require demolition because the mark returned to the house from which they were taken.
after the removal and the plastering. Or after scraping the mark alone in a case where the mark faded or went away in the second week (above, halakhah 2).
like the purity of a person that we explained in every respect. Above 11:1.
and likewise stones that are removed from it after the quarantine etc.. As explained above 15:2.
it defiles people and vessels by touch, by carrying and by entering. But it does not defile by lying or sitting, unlike a leprous person and leprous garments (see above 10:11, 13:13).
like a leprous person. Above 10:12.
a curse. A malediction.

and all of them are sent outside the city, even if it is not walled. Like leprous garments (above 13:15), and unlike a leprous person, who is sent out only from walled cities (above 10:7; Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:1-2).
was he then pure?. But he was already impure while the house was in quarantine.

stones with the affliction in a quarantined house defile from behind them. Although a quarantined house defiles only from within, the stones in which the affliction is found also defile from their rear side.
a house that was a covering etc.. That spreads over the afflicted house.
and a person passed by an afflicted stone, it does not defile him; but if he left it there, it defiles him. Like a leprous person, who defiles by entering only when he stands in place (above 10:12).
for the seat of the afflicted is like him. Just as he is impure, so his seat is impure (ibid.).
among vessels. Such as those that become impure through leprosy of garments (see above 13:13).

one who spreads over an afflicted stone with his hand... is pure. For an afflicted object does not defile by tent-impurity as a corpse does (see Hilchot Tumat Met 1:10-11) but only by entering (and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 1:5 on the differences between tent-impurity and impurity of entering).
backwards. When his back enters the house first.

even if all of him entered except his nose, he is pure. He is not defiled until his whole body is inside the house, unlike one who enters in the usual way, who is defiled as soon as his head and most of his body enter (below in the next halakhah).
the Torah made impure the normal way of entering. The usual way people enter.
three by three. The minimum size of a garment to become impure (Hilchot Kelim 22:1; above 12:10).
that brought its airspace into an impure house became impure. A clay vessel becomes impure through its airspace (Hilchot Tumat Met 6:3; Hilchot Kelim 13:1).
but other vessels. Which become impure from their outer surface.
that entered undressed. Not worn on a person.
and his rings on his hands. Worn on his fingers.

the time it takes a person to recline and eat three eggs' worth of wheat bread with a relish. The amount of time it takes to recline and eat wheat bread the size of about three eggs, together with food eaten with bread (in which case the eating is quick and does not require much chewing; Commentary on the Mishnah, Negaim 13:9).
but to set a measure for one who lies down like one who eats. One who lies down must launder his clothes only if he stayed in the house as long as an eater stays there.
and his vessels. His clothes.
but a gentile does not receive impurity. Although the vessels on him become impure, he himself does not receive impurity (see Hilchot Tumat Met 1:13-14).
and his rings on his hands. Worn on his fingers.
only his hands became impure. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot (8:2) explains that this is impurity of rabbinic origin.

a tightly sealed vessel in a corpse's tent saves. A vessel placed in a corpse's tent with a tight, secure cover over it saves its contents from becoming impure, provided it is a clay vessel or a vessel that cannot become impure at all (see Hilchot Tumat Met 21:1).
a covered vessel saves in an afflicted house. If this vessel is in the afflicted house, it saves even when its cover is not tight and secure.

and everything that saves by being covered in a corpse's tent. Such as a tent that interposes against the impurity, so that it protects what is inside it by a cover alone, even without a tight seal (ibid.).
and the like. Vessels that cannot become impure.

the pit and the hadut. These save in a corpse's tent by a cover alone (Hilchot Tumat Met 21:6-7); a hadut is a kind of pool whose walls rise above the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Rosh Hashanah 3:5 and elsewhere).
a name used for more than one thing. A name shared by several things.
ayin. Color.
in order to warn them against slander. For the details of the prohibition of slander and gossip, see Hilchot De'ot 7:1-6.
and she put herself at risk to save him from the sea. When he was placed in the basket at the edge of the Nile (see Exodus 2:3-9).
but an error in which he equated him with the other prophets. See Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 7:6 regarding the differences between the prophecy of Moses our teacher and that of the other prophets.
therefore one who wishes to direct his ways rightly should keep far from sitting with them and from speaking with them. See also Hilchot De'ot 6:1.
vanity. Emptiness.
atak. Harsh, insolent speech.
a blemish. A flaw; a doubt cast on something.
as it is said, 'And they mocked the messengers of God' etc.. See also Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:11.
and deny the fundamental principle. The Master of the world (and see also Hilchot De'ot 7:3).
and they were guilty. They slandered, they falsely accused.
they set their mouth against the heavens. They speak against God and His angels.
sitting on corners. Idle sitting at the corners of the town or street.

He helps them and gives them merit through it, as it is said, 'Then they that feared the Lord spoke' etc.. And the verse continues, 'and the Lord listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the Lord and who think upon His name'; from this we learn that a book is written to their credit from the conversation of those who fear the Lord.
